questions.stem: A 31 year old Black Caribbean man has 3 months of a dry cough, breathlessness on exertion, tiredness and 4 kg weight loss. He has no night sweats and has never smoked. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. His chest is clear. A chest X-ray is shown (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lung fields.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy in a young Afro-Caribbean adult with dry cough and fatigue is sarcoidosis; malignancy and TB more often cause unilateral nodes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Young Afro-Caribbean adult, dry cough, fatigue, symmetrical hilar nodes.

elim: Gives asymmetrical mediastinal nodes with night sweats and itching.
Needs an antigen exposure and does not cause hilar nodes.
Unilateral hilar mass in an older smoker.
Upper lobe cavitation with fever and night sweats; nodes usually unilateral.

steps.x: E: Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis: Afro-Caribbean, age 20 to 40, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 10 day history of fever, painful swollen ankles and knees, and tender red lumps on both shins. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. She has no cough. Her throat swab is negative. A chest X-ray is requested.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?
questions.e: Fever, erythema nodosum and polyarthralgia complete Löfgren's syndrome with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on chest X-ray?

clues: tender red lumps on both shins
steps.x: Fever + erythema nodosum + polyarthralgia = Löfgren's.

elim: Seen in heart failure or lupus, not this picture.
Possible in other causes of erythema nodosum, but with fever and arthritis Löfgren's is most likely.

steps.x: A: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Löfgren's syndrome: fever, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum and polyarthralgia.

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with known pulmonary sarcoidosis has had two episodes of dizziness and one blackout this month. His pulse rate is 38 bpm and regular, BP 108/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His ECG is shown (see item resources). He takes no medicines.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Complete heart block: P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Cardiac sarcoidosis infiltrates the conducting system and causes heart block (and arrhythmias); in a 38 year old with sarcoidosis this is the most likely cause.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
Young man with sarcoidosis and complete heart block.

elim: Sarcoidosis can raise calcium, but this rarely causes complete heart block.
He is 38; granulomatous infiltration of the conducting system is far more likely.
Does not cause persistent complete heart block.

steps.x: A: Cardiac sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis can involve the heart; conduction block is the classic sign.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with sarcoidosis has woken with drooping of the right side of her face. She cannot close her right eye fully. Her limbs, speech and other cranial nerves are normal. Her temperature is 36.8°C and BP 122/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination of her face?
o: Ptosis with a dilated right pupil
Vesicles in the right ear canal
questions.e: Sarcoidosis causes a lower motor neurone facial palsy, so the forehead is also weak; forehead sparing would suggest a stroke.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination of her face?

clues: cannot close her right eye fully
steps.x: Sarcoid facial nerve palsy is a lower motor neurone lesion.

elim: The droop is on the right.
A third nerve palsy, not facial nerve.
Forehead sparing suggests an upper motor neurone lesion such as stroke.
Suggests Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV), not sarcoidosis.

steps.x: E: Weakness of the right forehead. Sarcoidosis: facial nerve palsy (LMN, forehead involved).

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray, fever of 38.0°C and painful ankles. Her oxygen saturation is 98% breathing air. Her serum calcium is normal. She has no cough. She is examined fully.
questions.q: Which is the most likely skin finding?
o: Purpuric rash on the buttocks and legs
Tender red nodules on the shins
questions.e: Erythema nodosum (tender red shin nodules) with fever, polyarthralgia and BHL makes Löfgren's syndrome.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely skin finding?
BHL + fever + arthralgia: complete Löfgren's.

elim: Erythema multiforme, usually after HSV or drugs.

steps.x: E: Tender red nodules on the shins. Erythema nodosum (painful shin rash) is a skin feature of sarcoidosis and part of Löfgren's.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man with pulmonary sarcoidosis has 3 weeks of thirst, passing large volumes of urine, constipation and low mood. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg. Blood tests are sent.
questions.q: Which set of results is most likely?
questions.e: Granulomas make active vitamin D independent of PTH, so calcium is high and PTH appropriately suppressed; high PTH would mean hyperparathyroidism.

steps.x: The question asks: Which set of results is most likely?
Symptoms of hypercalcaemia in sarcoidosis.

elim: Primary hyperparathyroidism; in sarcoidosis PTH is suppressed.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism, as in vitamin D deficiency or CKD.
Does not explain his symptoms of hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: B: High calcium, low PTH. Sarcoidosis causes PTH-independent hypercalcaemia via ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has 2 months of a dry cough and breathlessness. Her temperature is 36.9°C and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. She has a violaceous plaque on her nose. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Her full blood count is normal.
questions.q: Which blood test result is most likely to be raised?
questions.e: Serum ACE is raised in sarcoidosis, reflecting granuloma burden; it supports but does not prove the diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which blood test result is most likely to be raised?
Lupus pernio + BHL = sarcoidosis.

elim: Raised in vasculitis such as GPA.

steps.x: D: Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme. Sarcoidosis bloods: raised serum ACE, raised calcium, raised ESR.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has 2 months of painless swelling in front of both ears and a dry mouth. She also has aching joints and a dry cough. Her temperature is 37.4°C. Both parotid glands are firm and enlarged. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral painless parotid swelling with polyarthralgia and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is sarcoidosis; Sjögren's does not cause BHL.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: painless swelling in front of both ears
steps.x: Bilateral parotid swelling + polyarthralgia + BHL.

elim: Painful, short-lived parotitis with fever; no hilar nodes.
A single slow-growing lump, not bilateral swelling with BHL.
Dry mouth and parotid swelling, but bilateral hilar nodes point to sarcoidosis.

steps.x: D: Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis: bilateral parotid swelling (granulomatous infiltration) and polyarthralgia.

questions.stem: A 27 year old Black British woman has a chest X-ray as part of a visa medical. She has no symptoms and examination is normal. The X-ray shows symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with clear lungs. Her serum ACE is raised and her calcium is normal. Her sister has a similar condition.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Asymptomatic symmetrical BHL with raised ACE in a young Black woman with a family history is classic stage 1 sarcoidosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: Her sister has a similar condition
steps.x: Young Black woman, family history, symmetrical BHL, raised ACE.

elim: Usually asymmetrical nodes with B symptoms.
Unusual at 27 in a non-smoker, and typically unilateral.
Usually symptomatic with unilateral nodes; ACE is not typically raised.
Needs heavy silica exposure and gives upper zone nodules.

steps.x: D: Sarcoidosis. Risk factors: Afro-Caribbean ethnicity, family history; age 20 to 40.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had sarcoidosis for 3 years and does not attend follow-up. He now has severe colicky right loin pain radiating to the groin. Urine dipstick shows blood. CT shows a 6 mm calcium stone in the right ureter. His serum calcium is 2.94 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his stone?
o: Urinary tract infection with urease-producing bacteria
questions.e: Granuloma 1-alpha-hydroxylase raises calcium absorption, causing hypercalcaemia, hypercalciuria and calcium stones.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of his stone?
Known sarcoidosis + high calcium + calcium stone.

elim: Inherited, presents young, with hexagonal crystals and normal calcium.
Uric acid stones are radiolucent and calcium is normal.
Also causes stones, but his known sarcoidosis explains the hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: B: Hypercalciuria from sarcoidosis. Hypercalcaemia (and hypercalciuria) is a complication of sarcoidosis.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman was diagnosed with sarcoidosis 16 years ago and stopped attending clinic. She now has 2 years of worsening breathlessness and a dry cough. Her oxygen saturation is 91% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral upper zone fibrosis with hilar retraction and no lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening breathlessness?
questions.e: Untreated progressive sarcoidosis can scar the lungs irreversibly (Scadding stage 4), typically upper zone; loss of nodes here is not resolution.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her worsening breathlessness?
Untreated, long-standing sarcoidosis with fibrosis.

elim: Gives variable wheeze, not upper zone fibrosis.
Basal predominant; she has known sarcoidosis with upper zone change.
Would give enlarging nodes; hers have gone.
Nodes have gone, but fibrosis means progression, not resolution.

steps.x: D: Progression to pulmonary fibrosis. Progressive granulomatous inflammation can lead to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis (stage 4).

questions.stem: A 47 year old man is brought in confused and dehydrated. He has had 6 weeks of a dry cough. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 108/70 mmHg. Adjusted calcium is 3.3 mmol/L, PTH is suppressed and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is raised. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his hypercalcaemia?
questions.e: Low PTH with raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and BHL is granulomatous (sarcoid) hypercalcaemia; myeloma and metastases do not raise active vitamin D.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his hypercalcaemia?
PTH-independent hypercalcaemia with high active vitamin D and BHL.

elim: PTH would be low but 1,25-vitamin D would not be raised.
Causes hypercalcaemia with low PTH but not raised 1,25-vitamin D or BHL.
PTH would be raised, not suppressed.
Raises 25-hydroxyvitamin D; BHL points to granulomas.

steps.x: D: Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis causes raised serum ACE and hypercalcaemia.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man with sarcoidosis has 2 days of a painful red right eye with blurred vision and pain on looking at lights. There is redness concentrated around the cornea and the pupil is small and irregular. An ophthalmologist performs a slit-lamp examination.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on slit-lamp examination?
o: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber
Dilated fixed pupil with a hazy cornea
Sectoral redness of the episclera only
questions.e: Anterior uveitis shows inflammatory cells and flare in the anterior chamber; a fixed dilated pupil suggests acute glaucoma.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on slit-lamp examination?
Painful red eye, photophobia, small irregular pupil = anterior uveitis.

elim: Episcleritis, which does not affect vision.

steps.x: A: Cells and flare in the anterior chamber. Sarcoidosis is associated with anterior uveitis.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue, a dry cough, aching in several joints and 3 kg weight loss. She has had a painful red eye treated with steroid drops. Her temperature is 37.2°C and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with mid zone reticulonodular shadowing.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dry cough, fatigue, polyarthralgia, anterior uveitis and BHL with interstitial shadowing is multisystem sarcoidosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: fatigue, a dry cough, aching in several joints
painful red eye treated with steroid drops
steps.x: Multisystem: lungs, joints, eyes, nodes.

elim: Can cause lung disease, but not BHL with uveitis.
Gives pleurisy and rash rather than hilar nodes and uveitis.
Night sweats and upper lobe disease; nodes usually unilateral.

steps.x: C: Sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis is multisystem: dry cough, fatigue, uveitis, polyarthralgia, weight loss.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has firm, purple, raised plaques on her nose and cheeks and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. She has a mild dry cough. Her respiratory physician wants tissue to confirm the diagnosis by the least invasive route.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Biopsy of an accessible skin lesion (lupus pernio) showing non-caseating granulomas confirms sarcoidosis with the least risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

clues: purple, raised plaques on her nose
steps.x: Tissue is needed; an accessible lesion is present.

elim: More invasive than sampling an accessible skin lesion.
Far too invasive when skin is available.
Supportive only; it does not confirm the diagnosis.

steps.x: A: Biopsy of the skin lesion. Biopsy of lung, lymph node or skin showing non-caseating granulomas is definitive.

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has 2 months of a dry cough, fatigue and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray. His temperature is 37.0°C and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His GP sends blood tests while awaiting a respiratory appointment.
questions.q: Which set of blood results is most likely?
o: Normal ACE, low calcium and normal ESR
Raised ACE, raised calcium and raised ESR
questions.e: Sarcoidosis raises serum ACE (granuloma burden), calcium (ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase) and ESR (inflammation); PTH is suppressed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which set of blood results is most likely?
Suspected sarcoidosis: what do the bloods show?

elim: Does not fit active granulomatous disease.

steps.x: C: Raised ACE, raised calcium and raised ESR. Bloods: raised ACE, raised calcium, raised ESR.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has biopsy-proven sarcoidosis with a dry cough and breathlessness. His chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular infiltrates in both mid zones. There is no fibrosis or volume loss.
questions.q: Which Scadding stage is this?
questions.e: BHL with interstitial infiltrates is Scadding stage 2; infiltrates without nodes would be stage 3.

steps.x: The question asks: Which Scadding stage is this?

clues: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with reticulonodular infiltrates
steps.x: Nodes plus infiltrates.
C: Stage 2. Scadding: 0 normal, 1 BHL, 2 BHL + infiltrates, 3 infiltrates only, 4 fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has had sarcoidosis for 20 years. Her chest X-ray shows coarse fibrotic shadowing in both upper zones with upward hilar retraction, volume loss and traction bronchiectasis. Hilar lymph nodes are no longer enlarged.

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Bilateral upper zone fibrosis with volume loss.

questions.q: Which Scadding stage is this?
questions.e: Fibrosis with volume loss and traction bronchiectasis is Scadding stage 4, which is irreversible.

steps.x: The question asks: Which Scadding stage is this?
Established fibrosis.

elim: Infiltrates without BHL but no established fibrosis.

steps.x: E: Stage 4. Stage 4: diffuse or advanced pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has cutaneous sarcoidosis confirmed on skin biopsy. She has no cough or breathlessness and her oxygen saturation is 99% breathing air. Her chest X-ray shows no hilar lymphadenopathy and clear lung fields.
questions.q: Which Scadding stage is this?
questions.e: A normal chest X-ray is Scadding stage 0, even with extrapulmonary disease such as skin sarcoidosis.

steps.x: The question asks: Which Scadding stage is this?

clues: no hilar lymphadenopathy and clear lung fields
steps.x: Proven sarcoidosis with a normal chest X-ray.
A: Stage 0. Stage 0: normal chest radiograph.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray with clear lung fields. Transbronchial biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. He has a mild dry cough. His calcium and lung function are normal.
questions.q: Which Scadding stage is this?
questions.e: BHL alone is Scadding stage 1; with normal calcium and lung function it is usually monitored as it may resolve.

steps.x: The question asks: Which Scadding stage is this?

clues: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray with clear lung fields
steps.x: Nodes only, lungs clear.

elim: Requires infiltrates as well as BHL.

steps.x: B: Stage 1. Stage 1: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy alone (often managed with monitoring).

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has stage 2 pulmonary sarcoidosis. She is breathless climbing two flights of stairs. Her respiratory physician needs to measure how much her lung function is affected before deciding whether to treat.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
o: Full pulmonary function tests including TLCO
questions.e: Pulmonary function tests (spirometry, lung volumes, TLCO) show the restrictive defect and guide whether treatment is needed.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

clues: how much her lung function is affected
steps.x: Measuring functional lung impairment.

elim: Diagnosis is already confirmed; this does not measure function.
Assesses the heart, not lung function.
Reflects granuloma burden but not lung function.

steps.x: D: Full pulmonary function tests including TLCO. PFTs monitor disease and show a restrictive pattern.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has Löfgren's syndrome with fever, erythema nodosum, painful ankles and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Her calcium, eyes and lung function are normal. Her temperature is 37.9°C and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: NSAIDs for symptoms, reassurance and monitoring
questions.e: Löfgren's syndrome usually resolves on its own, so NSAIDs for joint pain with reassurance and monitoring are enough; steroids need a specific indication.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: calcium, eyes and lung function are normal
steps.x: Löfgren's with no organ-threatening features.

elim: For severe organ-threatening disease, not Löfgren's.
Used for cardiac or refractory disease.
Not needed: no lung, eye, calcium, neurological or cardiac indication.

steps.x: B: NSAIDs for symptoms, reassurance and monitoring. Mild stage 1/2: reassurance and monitoring, as it may resolve spontaneously.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man with sarcoidosis has thirst and constipation. His adjusted calcium is 3.0 mmol/L on two occasions. He is drinking well, his creatinine is normal and his oxygen saturation is 96% breathing air. He takes no vitamin D supplements.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment for the cause of his hypercalcaemia?
questions.e: Hypercalcaemia is an indication for oral corticosteroids, which suppress granuloma 1-alpha-hydroxylase; thiazides and calcium supplements worsen it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment for the cause of his hypercalcaemia?
Hypercalcaemia is an indication for steroids in sarcoidosis.
D: Oral prednisolone. Steroids are indicated for lung disease, uveitis, hypercalcaemia, neurological or cardiac involvement.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with sarcoidosis rings her GP. Since yesterday her left eye is painful and red, her vision is blurred and bright light hurts. She has no discharge. Her other eye is normal.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Suspected anterior uveitis needs same-day ophthalmology for slit-lamp examination and steroid treatment to protect vision.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Painful red eye with photophobia in sarcoidosis = anterior uveitis.

elim: For bacterial conjunctivitis, which gives discharge with normal vision.

steps.x: D: Same-day referral to ophthalmology. Anterior uveitis is associated with sarcoidosis and is an indication for steroids.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with biopsy-proven sarcoidosis develops a left lower motor neurone facial palsy. His MRI shows no stroke. His temperature is 36.8°C and BP 126/80 mmHg. His chest X-ray shows stage 1 disease and his lung function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: No treatment, as stage 1 disease resolves
Surgical decompression of the facial nerve
questions.e: Neurological involvement is an indication for corticosteroids even when lung disease is mild; azathioprine is second-line.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?
Neurological sarcoidosis.

elim: Neurological involvement needs treatment regardless of stage.
Second-line if steroids fail or are contraindicated.
For Ramsay Hunt or HSV; he has sarcoidosis.

steps.x: C: Oral prednisolone. Neurological involvement is an indication for oral corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has cardiac sarcoidosis with episodes of second-degree heart block and ventricular ectopics on Holter monitoring. Cardiac MRI shows patchy late gadolinium enhancement. She has started oral prednisolone. Her cardiologist wants to add a steroid-sparing agent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional drug?
questions.e: Cardiac sarcoidosis is treated with steroids plus oral methotrexate; antiarrhythmics and devices treat the rhythm but not the granulomas.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate additional drug?
Cardiac involvement needs immunosuppression.

elim: An antiarrhythmic, not a treatment of the granulomatous disease.
Used for skin sarcoidosis, not the standard for cardiac disease.

steps.x: D: Oral methotrexate. Cardiac involvement specifically: oral methotrexate.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has progressive stage 3 pulmonary sarcoidosis. He relapsed on prednisolone and was switched to oral azathioprine 9 months ago. His FVC has fallen from 72% to 61% predicted and his breathlessness is worse. There is no infection.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Sarcoidosis refractory to steroids and azathioprine can be treated with combination methotrexate and azathioprine.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Refractory to steroids and azathioprine.

elim: An IPF antifibrotic, not treatment for active sarcoidosis.

steps.x: A: Add oral methotrexate to azathioprine. Severe or refractory disease: combine methotrexate and azathioprine.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman has symptomatic stage 2 sarcoidosis with falling lung function. She has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, severe osteoporosis with two vertebral fractures and had steroid-induced psychosis in the past. Her calcium is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Azathioprine is used when steroids fail or are contraindicated, as here; she still needs treatment because her lung function is falling.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
Treatment needed but steroids are contraindicated.

elim: Does not treat granulomatous lung disease.
First-line normally, but contraindicated by her diabetes, osteoporosis and psychosis.

steps.x: B: Oral azathioprine. Second-line: oral azathioprine if refractory to steroids or steroids are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 46 year old man with stage 3 sarcoidosis rings 111. Over 2 days he has become breathless talking and walking across a room. His home oxygen saturation is 86% breathing air, from his usual 95%. He feels frightened.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Double his prednisolone at home and review in a week
questions.e: Severe breathlessness with new hypoxia in sarcoidosis needs urgent hospital assessment (advanced disease, infection, PE).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Severe breathlessness with new hypoxia.

elim: He needs assessment for causes such as infection or PE first.

steps.x: E: Urgent same-day hospital assessment. Severe breathlessness indicates advanced lung involvement and needs urgent assessment.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has stage 1 sarcoidosis found on a chest X-ray. She has no symptoms, normal calcium, normal eyes and normal lung function. She is not being treated. She asks how she will be followed up.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?
o: Periodic symptom review with lung function and chest X-ray
questions.e: Untreated mild sarcoidosis is monitored by symptoms, lung function and imaging, since it may resolve or progress.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?

clues: how she will be followed up
steps.x: Untreated mild disease that may resolve or progress.

elim: Disease can progress, so she needs monitoring.

steps.x: E: Periodic symptom review with lung function and chest X-ray. Ongoing monitoring by lung function and symptoms.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. She has a mild dry cough and painful red lumps on her shins. A transbronchial lymph node biopsy shows tight collections of cells without central necrosis. Ziehl-Neelsen staining and fungal stains are negative.
questions.q: Which best describes the cells making up these lesions?
o: Eosinophils and mast cells around a central abscess
Epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes
questions.e: Sarcoid granulomas are non-caseating aggregates of epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes, formed against an unknown antigen.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the cells making up these lesions?

clues: Ziehl-Neelsen staining and fungal stains are negative
steps.x: Non-caseating granulomas with infection excluded.

elim: An allergic or parasitic picture, not a granuloma.

steps.x: B: Epithelioid macrophages and multinucleate giant cells surrounded by lymphocytes. Non-caseating granulomas: activated macrophages, epithelioid cells and giant cells ringed by lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man with sarcoidosis has an adjusted calcium of 2.92 mmol/L. He has thirst, polyuria and constipation and takes no supplements. His 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal. A medical student asks how the granulomas raise his calcium.
questions.q: Which result best supports the mechanism?
questions.e: Granuloma macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rises and PTH is suppressed, increasing gut calcium absorption.

steps.x: The question asks: Which result best supports the mechanism?

clues: how the granulomas raise his calcium
steps.x: Granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D themselves.

elim: Points to vitamin D deficiency or CKD.

steps.x: B: Raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D with suppressed PTH. Ectopic 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts vitamin D to its active form independent of renal regulation.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with sarcoidosis has serial serum ACE measurements. She has stage 2 disease with a dry cough and breathlessness on exertion. Her ACE was high at diagnosis and fell as her hilar nodes and lung infiltrates improved on prednisolone.
questions.q: Which best explains the changes in her serum ACE?
o: ACE is made by fibrotic lung tissue
It reflects her serum calcium only
It reflects the total burden of active granulomas
Prednisolone directly destroys ACE in the blood
questions.e: Epithelioid cells in granulomas make ACE, so serum ACE reflects granuloma burden and falls as disease responds.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best explains the changes in her serum ACE?

clues: fell as her hilar nodes and lung infiltrates improved
steps.x: ACE tracks disease activity.

elim: Calcium and ACE are separate effects of granulomas.
Steroids shrink granulomas, which lowers ACE production.
ACE in sarcoidosis comes from granulomas, not the kidney.

steps.x: C: It reflects the total burden of active granulomas. Raised serum ACE reflects granuloma activity/burden.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man has symmetrically enlarged hilar lymph nodes on both sides on chest X-ray. He has a mild dry cough and no night sweats or weight loss. His physician explains that this pattern favours sarcoidosis over lymphoma, lung cancer or TB.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the enlarged hilar nodes in sarcoidosis?
o: Granulomatous infiltration of the hilar and mediastinal nodes
Metastatic spread from a primary tumour
Right heart failure raising venous pressure
questions.e: Sarcoid BHL is due to non-caseating granulomas in the hilar and mediastinal nodes; malignancy and infection usually cause unilateral nodes.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of the enlarged hilar nodes in sarcoidosis?

clues: symmetrically enlarged hilar lymph nodes on both sides
steps.x: Bilateral and symmetrical = systemic granulomatous process.

elim: Typical of TB; sarcoid granulomas are non-caseating.
Would be unilateral and follow infection.
Causes large pulmonary arteries, not lymph nodes.

steps.x: B: Granulomatous infiltration of the hilar and mediastinal nodes. BHL reflects granulomatous infiltration of nodes; bilateral distinguishes it from the unilateral nodes of malignancy or infection.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has fever, erythema nodosum, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Her temperature is 37.8°C and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. She is worried she will need long-term treatment like her uncle, who has lung fibrosis from sarcoidosis.
questions.q: Which best describes the outlook for her presentation?
o: A high rate of spontaneous resolution with a good prognosis
questions.e: Löfgren's syndrome is an acute immune-complex-mediated presentation that usually resolves spontaneously within about 2 years.

steps.x: The question asks: Which best describes the outlook for her presentation?
Löfgren's: acute presentation.
A: A high rate of spontaneous resolution with a good prognosis. Löfgren's is an acute, immune-complex-mediated presentation with a good prognosis.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man with symptomatic stage 2 sarcoidosis starts oral prednisolone. Six months later his cough has improved, his infiltrates have cleared and his lung function has risen. He asks how the tablets work.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of benefit?
o: Suppression of T-cell and macrophage activity in granulomas
questions.e: Corticosteroids suppress the T cells and macrophages driving granulomas, reducing organ damage and progression to irreversible stage 4 fibrosis.
